How to read the numbers

cells.text: Renewal date minus today; negative means past due

text.text: Devices behind on patches
Backups not healthy
The first 30 days decide whether a new client trusts you. Onboarding finds everything you will be responsible for and fixes the dangerous things first.
Week one: discover
Walk the office: network closet, printers, server, internet connection, labels
Collect admin credentials into your password vault; change shared ones
Install the monitoring agent and endpoint protection on every computer
Add each device here with serial, user, operating system and warranty date
Record the internet provider, domain registrar, email platform and line-of-business software with their support numbers
Week two: stabilize
Patch every device to Current; anything on an unsupported system becomes a replacement on the renewal plan.
Confirm backups run for servers and cloud mail; run the first restore test.
Remove old accounts of people who left.
Turn on multi-factor sign-in for email and remote access.
Week three and four: agree the routine
Set the patch window with the client (for example Wednesday after 8 pm).
Agree who may request changes and who approves purchases.
Explain how to raise a ticket and the response targets.

cells.text: Something is slow or broken with a workaround

text.text: Close onboarding

Move the client from Onboarding to Healthy when devices are patched, backups are tested and the client has signed off the device list. Book a 30-day check-in, and ask the client then what still annoys them. The answers often point to one small fix, such as a printer that drops off the network, that wins more goodwill than any report.
Example
Pelican Bay Realty started eight days ago. The new sales laptop is set up, the mail migration cutover is scheduled this week, and their old shared printer account is on the list to remove.
Clients judge you on how fast someone answers and how often the same thing breaks. Triage sets the priority honestly and makes sure the clock is visible.

Set

by impact and urgency, not by who shouted.

Send the first reply and fill
First response
with the time. Tick

if it was inside the target.

: Covered by the agreement or Billable.
Choosing priority

cells.text: Many people or a whole site

text.text: Keep tickets honest
A ticket waiting on the client moves to
Waiting on client
. Remind them twice over a week, then resolve with a note.
A ticket with no update in two working days gets a note and an update to the client, even if there is no news.
Hours go in when work happens, not at the end of the month.
Escalation
Urgent with no first response after 30 minutes: the service manager takes it.
Any suspected security incident: stop, isolate the device, call the owner. Do not delete evidence.
The same problem three times in a month on one device: open a Project ticket to fix the cause.
Weekly review
Response targets met this week, by priority
Tickets reopened after resolving
Clients with the most tickets and what they have in common
Billable hours not yet invoiced
Example

Larkin & Boyd's backup alert was answered after the target, so Response target met is unticked. In the weekly review the team finds the alert arrives by email at night, and changes it to page the on-call tech.
Most outages and breaches start on a device that was not patched, not backed up or too old. A clear device list with patch and backup status lets you see risk before it bites.
Patch status, in plain words

cells.text: The vendor no longer ships fixes

text.text: The weekly patch routine
Approve updates after a few days' delay, so bad updates are caught by others first.
Patch in the client's agreed window; servers one at a time.
Next morning, update
Patch status
and
Last patched
from the report.
Anything still Missing patches after two windows becomes a ticket.
Backups
Check the backup report every morning. Warning or Failed gets an Alert ticket.
Test a restore once a quarter for each client, and record it as a Maintenance job. A backup is not real until you have restored from it.
Devices marked Not covered should hold no company data.
Planning replacements
Laptops and desktops: plan for four to five years.
Servers, firewalls and switches: five to seven years, or when support ends.
Watch
Warranty ends
; the dashboard shows what ends in the next 90 days.
Put each replacement in the client's renewal conversation with a price, so it is budgeted rather than a surprise.
Retiring a device
Data backed up or moved
Removed from monitoring, endpoint protection and the directory
Drive wiped or destroyed, with a note of how
Status set to Retired with the date
Example

Hawthorne Veterinary renews this week and is At risk. Their imaging workstation runs an unsupported system and the imaging software crashes on it. Replacing it is already scheduled; until then it is kept off email and web browsing.
A renewal is the one meeting a year where the client looks at everything you did. Bring evidence, a plan for next year and an honest price.

What to bring

cells.text: Tickets handled, response targets met, longest outage
Patching level, endpoint protection on every device, multi-factor sign-in, backup tests
Replacements due, projects suggested, rough cost
Seats, plan, included hours, any price change and why

text.text: Pricing
Price per seat or per device, plus servers and network gear.
If billable hours were high every month, offer included project hours instead.
Explain any increase with the change in seats, tools or labor, never as a surprise.
Clients at risk
Mark a client
At risk
when they complain about the same thing twice, miss invoices, or go quiet. The account owner calls them within a week, and the problem gets a named fix with a date.
After the meeting
New renewal date, fee and seats entered
Agreed projects added as Maintenance jobs or Project tickets
Status set to Healthy or At risk, honestly
Thank-you note with the agreed plan in writing
Ending a client

Hand over admin access, documentation and the device list. Set the status to Ended and keep the history. Leave on good terms: a clean handover is often the reason a client comes back, or recommends you to someone else.
Example
Granger Family Dental's renewal date passed six days ago without a signed agreement. The owner calls this week with a summary of the year and a quote to replace two front-desk computers.

This workspace sits beside your remote monitoring and ticketing tools. Those tools raise alerts and run scripts; this is where the owner and the techs see each client as a whole: what they pay for, what state their devices are in, what is waiting, and what is coming up.
The lists

cells.text: Plan, agreement type, seats, monthly fee, project hours included, renewal date, open tickets, devices behind on patches, billable hours
Every laptop, server, firewall and switch with serial, user, operating system, patch status, last patched, backup state, endpoint protection and warranty
Type, priority, response target, first response, whether the target was met, due date, hours and whether the work is covered or billable
Patch windows, backup restore tests, hardware swaps, migrations and security reviews, with the number of devices covered

text.text: How the numbers work
Open tickets
counts New, In progress and Waiting on client.
Devices behind on patches
counts Missing patches and Unsupported OS. Pending reboot is shown on the dashboard but not counted, because it usually clears overnight.
Response target
comes from the priority: Urgent 1 hour, High 2, Normal 4, Low 8. Change the numbers to match your own agreements.
Billable hours
adds hours on tickets marked Billable, so project work outside the agreement is not forgotten on the invoice.
Your first week
Enter each client with plan, agreement type, seats, fee and renewal date.
Import devices from your monitoring tool: name, serial, user, operating system and warranty date. Then set patch and backup status from the latest reports.
Move open tickets in with their original opened time, so response targets are honest.
Put the next month of patch windows and restore tests under Maintenance.
The daily rhythm
First thing:
Tickets, Overdue and Due this week. Anything Urgent with no first response is handled before anything else.
Mid-morning:
dashboard lists Devices behind on patches and Backups not healthy. Failed backups become an Alert ticket.
End of day:
every ticket worked has hours entered and billing set.
Buttons
Ticket buttons resolve or reassign; maintenance buttons tick a job done and date it; client buttons open a new ticket or device already linked.
Example
Larkin & Boyd's office server shows Pending reboot and a failed backup. The backup alert is ticketed, the reboot goes into the patch window this week, and the restore test is booked for next week.
